clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive glycolytic enzymopathy producing chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia, often with associated myopathy
The A isoform predominates in red cells and muscle, so deficiency frequently combines haemolysis with exertional muscle symptoms and raised creatine kinase
Rhabdomyolysis may be provoked by febrile illness or vigorous exercise, sometimes as a presenting event
Some patients show growth retardation and dysmorphic features, reflecting the enzyme's wide tissue expression
Anaemia is Coombs-negative and the film lacks the spherocytes of membrane disease
Diagnosis depends on reduced red-cell aldolase activity and identification of an ALDOA mutation
Management is supportive with transfusion and folate, avoidance of exertional and febrile triggers of muscle breakdown, and splenectomy considered in severe transfusion-dependent haemolysis
reference.pathophysiology: Aldolase A catalyses the cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into the two triose phosphates that continue through glycolysis, the sole ATP source for the mature red cell. Reduced activity impairs glycolytic flux and energy generation, shortening red-cell survival and causing a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because the A isoenzyme is also highly expressed in skeletal muscle, deficiency additionally compromises muscle energy metabolism, predisposing to myopathy and exercise- or fever-induced rhabdomyolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Other glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies
additionalInvestigations: Creatine kinase and myoglobin, especially during muscle symptoms
Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Molecular testing of the ALDOA gene
redFlags: Acute rhabdomyolysis with risk of acute kidney injury
Severe neonatal or childhood jaundice requiring exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection
Progressive myopathy or failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on the severity of both the haemolytic anaemia and the muscle involvement; well-compensated cases fare well, whereas recurrent rhabdomyolysis and severe transfusion-dependent anaemia carry greater morbidity.
pitfalls: Missing the muscle component and attributing symptoms to a purely haematological disorder
Failing to check creatine kinase during febrile illness or after exercise
Not counselling patients to avoid exertional and febrile triggers of rhabdomyolysis
Overlooking transfusional iron overload during long-term follow-up
